messages.author: 1c3bff3a8f16c06b
messages.subject: correct Bayesian updating
parts:
Hi!

Bayesian updating is a great feature of Bayesian models, and when using INLA, I'd like to do it correctly.

In the example below, am I using the posteriors from model m1 correctly as priors for m2?  I want m2 to be the best model given the data that was used for m1 and m2.  (Of course, the old data might be long gone in a non-trivial example.)

library(INLA)
set.seed(1)
inla.seed = 2

# first data set is used with default priors to fit model m1
x <- 1:100
y <- 5 + 4 * x + rnorm(n=length(x), sd=3)
m1 <- inla(y ~ x, data=data.frame(x, y), control.compute=list(config=TRUE))

# set up priors for m2 fixed-effects parameters based on m1 posteriors
posterior.mean <- function(m, name) m$summary.fixed[name, "mean"]
posterior.prec <- function(m, name) 1/m$summary.fixed[name, "sd"]^2
fixed.priors <- list()
fixed.priors$mean = list()
fixed.priors$prec = list()
for (name in c("(Intercept)", "x")) {
    fixed.priors$mean[[name]] <- posterior.mean(m1, name)
    fixed.priors$prec[[name]] <- posterior.prec(m1, name)
}

# use points from posterior of precision as prior for m2
ih <- m1$internal.marginals.hyperpar[[1]]
table.string <- paste(c("table:", ih[,"x"], ih[,"y"]), collapse=" ")

# new data
x <- seq(from=1, to=100, by=0.5)
y <- 5 + 4 * x + rnorm(n=length(x), sd=3)

# update model with new data
m2 <- inla(y ~ x,
    data=data.frame(x, y),
    control.fixed=fixed.priors,
    control.family=list(hyper=list(prec=list(prior=table.string))))

Thanks!

-- 
  Ed

messages.author: 9940b4fcc153c7d7
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] correct Bayesian updating
parts:
Hi,

My thoughts on Bayesian updating: 

This is great in theory, but works poorly in practice. Any numerical algorithm chooses a fidelity of approximation of the posterior. Clever algorithms (MCMC/INLA/...) only has a good fidelity where the posterior has large values (to save computational time).

When you fit a second dataset, the posterior contribution from this may be somewhere else than the posterior for the first dataset. This means that the fidelity of the relevant part of the first posterior is extremely poor. And so, we cannot represent (with reasonable high fidelity) the prior for the second dataset.

However, if the second dataset is "very consistent" with the first dataset, only concentrating the distributions more, I think it can work. But you do not know this in advance. Additionally, if everything is Gaussian, it might work. 

The easiest way to compute Bayesian updating, I think, is to re-fit the entire dataset1 & dataset2 in a new joint model.

In your code example, I do not think you have taken the posterior correlations into account. E.g. the likelihood (family) parameter is correlated with the fixed effect for "x".

PS: I appreciate being corrected on this, as I have never tried Bayesian updating

Kind regards,
Haakon

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] correct Bayesian updating
parts: Hi, Haakon Bakka.  I've been thinking about one of your comments.
On Mon, Mar 26, 2018 at 1:08 AM, Haakon Bakka <ba...@r-inla.org> wrote:
...
In your code example, I do not think you have taken the posterior correlations into account. E.g. the likelihood (family) parameter is correlated with the fixed effect for "x".

I have been assuming all along that for multiple covariates I'll need to specify a prior for the correlation (or precision) matrix for the fixed effects.

I know that I can extract the estimated covariance matrix from a fitted model, so after getting a grip on the simple case, I planned to tackle a case like the one below, where x1 and x2 are correlated.  I don't yet know how to construct a prior for the next model using the posterior covariance matrix from the last model.  (Pointers are welcome!)

After thinking about it, though, I believe that if I learn how to do that, it does not address your concern quoted above.  I understand that different values of the coefficient for x (in my original example) have different likelihoods, but the posterior distribution for x's coefficient summarizes that relationship.

> library(INLA)

> x1 <- 1:10 + rnorm(10)

> x2 <- x1 + rnorm(10)

> cor(x1, x2)

[1] 0.9707002

> y <- 4 * x1 + 3 * x2

> r <- inla(y ~ x1 + x2 -1, data=data.frame(x1, x2, y),

    control.fixed=list(correlation.matrix=TRUE),

    control.inla=list(lincomb.derived.correlation.matrix=TRUE))

> r$misc$lincomb.derived.covariance.matrix

              x1            x2

x1  1.992026e-06 -2.016117e-06

x2 -2.016117e-06  2.096023e-06

> r$misc$lincomb.derived.correlation.matrix

           x1         x2

x1  1.0000000 -0.9866663

x2 -0.9866663  1.0000000

> 



--
  Ed Cashin <eca...@noserose.net>

messages.author: 9940b4fcc153c7d7
messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] correct Bayesian updating
parts:
I think you can deal with the Gaussian variables: The beta_j are correlated when they come from one model. This correlation matrix can be used in the next step.
- Note that correlation in beta_j and in x_j are related but not the same thing.

I also think you can deal with correlation between hyper-parameters (using the joint posterior). I have not seen the feature Haavard mentioned, but I am assuming it does this.

What I think is very hard to deal with is dependency (including correlation) between the hyper-parameters and the beta_j. For simple GLM models this could maybe be solved by making all parameters into hyper-parameters. For complex models, one could consider fixing the hyper-parameters and not doing inference on them in the second step (the second dataset).

Regards,
Haakon

parts:
Thanks for the interesting discussion.  In my simple example model, the only hyperparameter is the precision of the observed values for the response variable.  If the model does a good job of explaining the data x, then I would expect the residuals to be distributed normally with respect to x.  If residual analysis showed heteroscedascicity, I would infer that my choice of model was not appropriate.  That's a dependence between the hyperparameter and the covariate, though, not beta_j, so ... is there some other kind of dependence you're thinking of?

I bet a minimal example that shows the danger would help.  What is the most simple data generating process and (appropriate) model that demonstrates the kind of problematic dependence that you have in mind, one between the fixed-effect estimates and the hyperparameter estimates?  I can't think of one, but I'm not done reading the Wang, Yue, and Faraway book yet.

I think that the only way the concern could be specific to Bayesian updating and not model building in general is if there's something important in the model that is missing from the inla result or unsupported as a prior.  I'd be really interested to find out if there's some limitation like that, but I haven't encountered one yet.
On Wed, Mar 28, 2018 at 7:55 AM Haakon Bakka <ba...@r-inla.org> wrote:

I think you can deal with the Gaussian variables: The beta_j are correlated when they come from one model. This correlation matrix can be used in the next step.
- Note that correlation in beta_j and in x_j are related but not the same thing.

I also think you can deal with correlation between hyper-parameters (using the joint posterior). I have not seen the feature Haavard mentioned, but I am assuming it does this.

What I think is very hard to deal with is dependency (including correlation) between the hyper-parameters and the beta_j. For simple GLM models this could maybe be solved by making all parameters into hyper-parameters. For complex models, one could consider fixing the hyper-parameters and not doing inference on them in the second step (the second dataset).

Regards,
Haakon




On 27 March 2018 at 16:25, Ed Cashin <eca...@noserose.net> wrote:
Hi, Haakon Bakka.  I've been thinking about one of your comments.

On Mon, Mar 26, 2018 at 1:08 AM, Haakon Bakka <ba...@r-inla.org> wrote:
...  
In your code example, I do not think you have taken the posterior correlations into account. E.g. the likelihood (family) parameter is correlated with the fixed effect for "x".

I have been assuming all along that for multiple covariates I'll need to specify a prior for the correlation (or precision) matrix for the fixed effects.

I know that I can extract the estimated covariance matrix from a fitted model, so after getting a grip on the simple case, I planned to tackle a case like the one below, where x1 and x2 are correlated.  I don't yet know how to construct a prior for the next model using the posterior covariance matrix from the last model.  (Pointers are welcome!)

After thinking about it, though, I believe that if I learn how to do that, it does not address your concern quoted above.  I understand that different values of the coefficient for x (in my original example) have different likelihoods, but the posterior distribution for x's coefficient summarizes that relationship.

> library(INLA)

> x1 <- 1:10 + rnorm(10)

> x2 <- x1 + rnorm(10)

> cor(x1, x2)

[1] 0.9707002

> y <- 4 * x1 + 3 * x2

> r <- inla(y ~ x1 + x2 -1, data=data.frame(x1, x2, y),

    control.fixed=list(correlation.matrix=TRUE),

    control.inla=list(lincomb.derived.correlation.matrix=TRUE))

> r$misc$lincomb.derived.covariance.matrix

              x1            x2

x1  1.992026e-06 -2.016117e-06

x2 -2.016117e-06  2.096023e-06

> r$misc$lincomb.derived.correlation.matrix

           x1         x2

x1  1.0000000 -0.9866663

x2 -0.9866663  1.0000000

> 



--
  Ed Cashin <eca...@noserose.net>

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] correct Bayesian updating
parts:
It is not impossible to deal with the posterior "in its entirety", one way to do it is by posterior samples. Understanding the representation of the posterior made by INLA is nontrivial (a set of integration points and precision matrices). 

In other words, formulated in general, my point is:
- If you sample from the prior model, this is (almost) always defined with independent components. So, if you sample the hyperparameter to be 1.7, you sample the beta independently
- If you sample from the posterior, this is completely dependent (since you conditioned on some data), so if you sample the hyperparameter to be 1.7, you must sample the beta conditionally on this value

The reason most models are defined with independent prior components is that it is incredibly convenient. Specifying a prior model where the components have (any kind of) dependency is difficult. And I am no talking about inference now, merely the act of specifying the model, writing it down in a clean way. How would you make an interface for an algorithm that could cover every conceivable prior dependency?

This is why I was saying, in most cases, it might be easier to go back to the "independent prior components defined" model, and fit both the old and new data at once (which is not possible in the case you stated).

Kind regards,
Haakon
